text: SQL Auditing writes a log of who did what — but that log could theoretically be edited by someone with enough access. Ledger solves a stricter problem: cryptographically proving a table's history hasn't been tampered with.

Every change to a ledger table is appended to a tamper-evident history, and the database computes a cryptographic digest you can store outside the database to later verify nothing was altered, even by sysadmin.

Don't conflate this with Ledger or auditing. Change Tracking answers which rows changed since you last checked, for sync scenarios — lightweight, no cryptographic proof, not a security feature at all.
A real compliance scenario needs TDE, classification, masking, auditing, and Ledger together — each answering a different piece of the same question, none substituting for the others.
Auditing tells you what happened. Ledger proves the record is genuine. Change Tracking just tracks what's new. Chapter 6 is complete — next up, Chapter 7: Monitoring Azure SQL.
